title: Configuration and Storage
subtitle: ConfigMaps, Secrets, persistent volumes and namespace governance
description: Separate configuration from images, handle sensitive data safely, give workloads durable storage and keep shared namespaces under control.
outcomes: Inject configuration with ConfigMaps and Secrets
Enforce quotas and defaults per namespace

lessons.title: ConfigMaps
lessons.summary: Decouple configuration from images: create ConfigMaps, inject them as env vars or files, and freeze them with immutable.
objectives: Create a ConfigMap from literals, files and YAML
Consume it as environment variables and as a volume
Know which consumption method picks up updates

sections.title: Configuration outside the image
sections.body:
A **ConfigMap** stores non-confidential configuration as key/value pairs in the cluster. Pods consume it as environment variables, command-line arguments or files in a volume, so the same image runs unchanged in dev, staging and production.

A ConfigMap holds at most **1 MiB** and lives in a namespace; a Pod can only reference ConfigMaps from its own namespace. Never put passwords in one, use a Secret for that.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: Two ways to create a ConfigMap
sections.body: This is the command-line way to create a ConfigMap, followed by a declarative alternative. `kubectl create configmap app-config` builds it from a literal (`LOG_LEVEL=info`) and from a local file (`nginx.conf`), and `kubectl get ... -o yaml` prints back what the cluster stored. We show it first so you see that a ConfigMap is just named key/value data; look at how the file name became a key under `data`. The second half pipes a YAML manifest into `kubectl apply` to create `app-settings`.

sections.code:
kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info \
  --from-file=nginx.conf
kubectl get configmap app-config -o yaml

# or declaratively
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-settings
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  app.properties: |
    mode=production
    retries=3
EOF
sections.title: Creating a ConfigMap
sections.output:
configmap/app-config created
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-03-10T09:12:41Z"
  name: app-config
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "48213"
  uid: 7c1f0b52-6a3e-4d0e-9c64-2f1d8e5b9a10
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  nginx.conf: |
    server {
      listen 80;
      location / { return 200 "ok\n"; }
    }
configmap/app-settings created
sections.note: Values under `data` are always strings, so quote booleans and numbers. Use `binaryData` for non-UTF-8 content. `--from-file=nginx.conf` makes the file name the key and the file content the value.

sections.title: The app-settings manifest in full
sections.body: This is the full YAML file for the `app-settings` ConfigMap, the same object the previous command created, written as a manifest you can keep in Git and apply with `kubectl apply -f`. Look at the two kinds of keys under `data`: short values such as `LOG_LEVEL` and `FEATURE_X`, and multi-line blocks (`app.properties`, `nginx.conf`) introduced by `|` that become the content of whole files. Note the quotes around `"true"`, because every value is a string.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-settings
data:
  # simple key/value pairs
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  # file-style key: the whole block becomes one file's content
  app.properties: |
    mode=production
    retries=3
  nginx.conf: |
    server {
      listen 80;
      location / { return 200 "ok\n"; }
    }
immutable: false
sections.title: Complete ConfigMap manifest
sections.output: configmap/app-settings created
sections.note: Literal keys (LOG_LEVEL) suit environment variables; file-style keys (app.properties, nginx.conf) suit volume mounts.

sections.title: Checking what was stored
sections.body: These two commands list the ConfigMaps in the namespace and then show the details of `app-settings`. We use them to confirm the object exists and holds the data we expect before any Pod depends on it. In the output, check the DATA column (number of keys) and the `Data` section, which prints every key and its value in clear text.

sections.code:
kubectl get configmap
kubectl describe configmap app-settings
sections.title: Inspecting a ConfigMap
sections.output:
NAME               DATA   AGE
kube-root-ca.crt   1      21d
app-config         2      3m
app-settings       4      2m

Name:         app-settings
Namespace:    default
Labels:       <none>
Annotations:  <none>

Data
====
FEATURE_X:
----
true

LOG_LEVEL:
----
info

app.properties:
----
mode=production
retries=3

nginx.conf:
----
server {
  listen 80;
  location / { return 200 "ok\n"; }
}


BinaryData

Events:  <none>
sections.note: DATA counts keys. Unlike Secrets, describe prints the values in clear text.

sections.title: A Pod that consumes the ConfigMap
sections.body: This is a Pod manifest, saved as `cfg-demo.yaml` and applied with `kubectl apply -f cfg-demo.yaml`, that uses `app-settings` in three ways. `env` with `configMapKeyRef` injects one key as `LOG_LEVEL`, `envFrom` injects every key as variables, and the `configMap` volume mounted at `/etc/app` turns the `app.properties` key into a file. Its command prints the variables and the file, so `kubectl logs` shows whether it worked.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cfg-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "env | grep -E 'LOG|FEATURE'; cat /etc/app/app.properties; sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: LOG_LEVEL
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-settings
          key: LOG_LEVEL
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-settings
    volumeMounts:
    - name: cfg
      mountPath: /etc/app
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: cfg
    configMap:
      name: app-settings
      items:
      - key: app.properties
        path: app.properties
sections.title: Env vars and volume mounts
sections.output:
$ kubectl apply -f cfg-demo.yaml
pod/cfg-demo created
$ kubectl logs cfg-demo
LOG_LEVEL=info
FEATURE_X=true
mode=production
retries=3
sections.note: `env`/`envFrom` inject variables; the `configMap` volume projects each key as a file.

sections.title: Looking at the mounted files
sections.body: These commands run inside the running `cfg-demo` Pod to list the `/etc/app` directory and print the `app.properties` file. We do this to prove the ConfigMap key really became a file. In the output, notice that the file is a symlink into a `..data` directory, which is how Kubernetes swaps in updated content.

sections.code:
kubectl exec cfg-demo -- ls -l /etc/app
kubectl exec cfg-demo -- cat /etc/app/app.properties
sections.title: Files inside the container
sections.output:
total 0
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            21 Mar 10 09:20 app.properties -> ..data/app.properties
mode=production
retries=3
sections.note: Each key becomes a symlink into a timestamped ..data directory; the kubelet swaps that link atomically on updates.

sections.title: What the Pod sees
sections.body: This is not a file you create or apply. It is a plain-text summary of what the `cfg-demo` Pod sees: the contents of `/etc/app/app.properties` and the two environment variables injected from the ConfigMap. We show it so you can match each value back to the keys in `app-settings`.

sections.code:
# /etc/app/app.properties (inside the container)
mode=production
retries=3

# environment (env | grep -E 'LOG|FEATURE')
LOG_LEVEL=info
FEATURE_X=true
sections.title: Sample content as seen in the container
sections.note: Not applyable: this is what the Pod sees, not a manifest.

sections.title: Using a ConfigMap in a Deployment
sections.body: This is a Deployment manifest (`kubectl apply -f`) that runs two nginx replicas configured from `app-settings`. It sets `LOG_LEVEL` as an environment variable and mounts only the `nginx.conf` key as `/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`. Look at the `subPath` line: it lets you place one file into an existing directory, but files mounted this way do not receive later ConfigMap updates.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27-alpine
        env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-settings
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        volumeMounts:
        - name: conf
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
          subPath: nginx.conf
      volumes:
      - name: conf
        configMap:
          name: app-settings
sections.title: Deployment consuming a ConfigMap
sections.output: deployment.apps/web created
sections.note: This mount uses subPath, so edits to nginx.conf will NOT reach running Pods: restart them.

sections.title: Which consumption method updates?
head: Method
Updated after ConfigMap edit?
Notes
rows: Read once at container start; restart the Pod
Yes, eventually (kubelet sync, typically up to a minute or so)
Files are swapped via symlinks; the app must re-read them

sections.title: Locking a ConfigMap with immutable
sections.body: This is a small ConfigMap manifest, `app-config-v2`, with `immutable: true` on the last line. Immutable ConfigMaps cannot be edited after creation, which protects running Pods from accidental changes and reduces load on the API server. The output shows the error you get when you try to edit one anyway.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v2
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: warn
immutable: true
sections.title: Immutable ConfigMap sample
sections.output:
configmap/app-config-v2 created

# later, kubectl edit configmap app-config-v2 and saving a change:
error: configmaps "app-config-v2" is invalid: data: Forbidden: field is immutable when `immutable` is set
sections.note: Delete and recreate under a new name (app-config-v3) to change it, then point the Deployment at the new name.

sections.title: Immutable ConfigMaps
sections.body: Set `immutable: true` to forbid changes to `data`. This protects against accidental edits and reduces API server load because kubelets stop watching it. To change it you must delete and recreate it, so version the name (`app-config-v2`) and roll the Deployment to the new name.

sections.title: Config changes do not restart Pods
sections.body: Editing a ConfigMap does not roll a Deployment. Use `kubectl rollout restart deployment/NAME`, or version the ConfigMap name in the Pod template so a change triggers a rollout.

questions.question: How does a running container see an updated ConfigMap value?
options: Mounted files update eventually; env vars need a restart
questions.explain: Volume-projected files are refreshed by the kubelet; environment variables are fixed at container start.

questions.question: What is the size limit of a ConfigMap?
questions.explain: ConfigMap data is stored in etcd and capped at 1 MiB.

questions.question: What does immutable: true do?
options: Prevents changes to data; must be recreated to change
questions.explain: Immutable ConfigMaps cannot be edited, which prevents accidents and lowers watch load.

questions.question: A ConfigMap is mounted with subPath. After editing it, the file...
options: Stays stale until the Pod restarts
questions.explain: Containers using subPath volume mounts do not receive ConfigMap updates.

lessons.title: Secrets
lessons.summary: Store sensitive data the Kubernetes way, understand why base64 is not encryption, and handle Secrets safely.
objectives: Create Secrets of the common types
Consume Secrets as env vars and volumes
Explain why base64 offers no protection
Apply RBAC, encryption at rest and other safe-handling practices

sections.title: What a Secret is
sections.body:
A **Secret** holds a small amount of sensitive data such as a password, token or key. It is structurally like a ConfigMap, but the API treats it more carefully: it can be restricted by RBAC, kept out of logs and `kubectl describe` output, and encrypted at rest. Secrets are limited to **1 MiB**.

Values in `data` are **base64-encoded**. This is only an encoding so binary data fits in JSON/YAML. Anyone who can read the object can decode it in one command.

sections.title: Encoded versus decoded
sections.body: The same Secret as stored (`data`, base64) and as the application sees it (decoded). Encode with `echo -n 'S3cr3t!' | base64`, decode with `base64 -d`. Always use `-n` when encoding, or a trailing newline becomes part of the password.

sections.title: A Secret written as a manifest
sections.body: This is the YAML file for a Secret named `db-creds`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. The type `Opaque` means generic key/value data, and values under `data` must be base64-encoded (`YXBw` is `app`). Remember that base64 is only an encoding, not encryption, so anyone who can read this file can read the password.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  username: YXBw
  password: UzNjcjN0IQ==
sections.title: Opaque Secret manifest (base64 data)
sections.output: secret/db-creds configured
sections.note: Alternative: use `stringData:` with plaintext values and the API server encodes them for you on write.

sections.title: Skipping the manual base64 step
sections.body: This is another Secret manifest, `db-creds-plain`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. Instead of `data` it uses `stringData`, where you type plain values and the API server encodes them for you. We show it because it is the easiest way to write a Secret by hand; compare the `password` line with the base64 version above.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-creds-plain
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: app
  password: S3cr3t!
sections.title: Secret with stringData
sections.output: secret/db-creds-plain created
sections.note: stringData is write-only: kubectl get -o yaml returns it base64-encoded under data.

sections.title: How Secrets appear when you read them
sections.body: These three commands list Secrets, print `db-creds` as YAML, and describe it. We run them to see what Kubernetes reveals. In the output, look at the base64 values from `get -o yaml` versus the byte sizes only that `describe` shows.

sections.code:
kubectl get secret
kubectl get secret db-creds -o yaml
kubectl describe secret db-creds
sections.title: Reading Secrets
sections.output:
NAME         TYPE                             DATA   AGE
db-creds     Opaque                           2      5m
regcred      kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson   1      5m
web-tls      kubernetes.io/tls                2      5m

apiVersion: v1
data:
  password: UzNjcjN0IQ==
  username: YXBw
kind: Secret
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-03-10T09:30:02Z"
  name: db-creds
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "49110"
  uid: 3b9a1d7e-52f4-4c8a-b0a1-9d6e47c2f8a3
type: Opaque

Name:         db-creds
Namespace:    default
Labels:       <none>
Annotations:  <none>

Type:  Opaque

Data
====
password:  7 bytes
username:  3 bytes
sections.note: `get -o yaml` shows base64 values; `describe` deliberately shows only sizes.

sections.title: A Secret for private image registries
sections.body: This is a Secret manifest named `regcred` of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`, used to pull images from a private registry. It has one key, `.dockerconfigjson`, whose base64 value holds the registry login. A Pod references it with `imagePullSecrets`, as shown in the Deployment later in this lesson.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: regcred
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
data:
  .dockerconfigjson: eyJhdXRocyI6IHsicmVnaXN0cnkuZXhhbXBsZS5jb20iOiB7InVzZXJuYW1lIjogImJvdCIsICJwYXNzd29yZCI6ICJUT0tFTiIsICJhdXRoIjogIlltOTBPbFJQUzBWTyJ9fX0=
sections.title: Docker-registry Secret
sections.output: secret/regcred created
sections.note: Decoded, .dockerconfigjson is the JSON shown next.

sections.title: What is inside that long value
sections.body: This is the JSON you get after base64-decoding the `.dockerconfigjson` value from `regcred`. It is not applied anywhere; we show it so the long string is not a mystery. Look at the registry host key (`registry.example.com`) and the `username`, `password` and `auth` fields.

sections.title: Decoded .dockerconfigjson
sections.note: Use it in a Pod with `imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]`.

sections.title: The shape of a TLS Secret
sections.body: This is an illustrative manifest for a Secret named `web-tls` of type `kubernetes.io/tls`, used for HTTPS certificates. It must contain exactly the keys `tls.crt` (the certificate) and `tls.key` (the private key), both base64-encoded. The values are truncated here, so create the real one with `kubectl create secret tls`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: web-tls
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
  tls.crt: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJUSUZJQ0FURS0tLS0t...   # base64 of the PEM certificate
  tls.key: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBQUklWQVRFIEtFWS0tLS0t...   # base64 of the PEM private key
sections.title: TLS Secret layout
sections.note: Shown with truncated values, so it is not applyable. Create the real one with `kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key`.

sections.title: Checking a certificate inside the Secret
sections.body: This command reads the `tls.crt` key of `web-tls`, decodes it from base64 and shows the first two lines. We use it to verify that the Secret holds a real PEM certificate. The `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` line is the sign that it decoded correctly.

sections.code:
$ kubectl get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | head -2
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIDXTCCAkWgAwIBAgIJAL...
sections.title: Decoded TLS content
Creating Secrets from the command line
sections.body: These commands create the three Secrets used in this lesson without writing YAML: a generic one (`db-creds`), a TLS one (`web-tls`) and a registry one (`regcred`). The last line reads the password back and decodes it. Look at that last output: it shows how easy it is to recover a Secret value, which is why access to Secrets must be restricted.

sections.code:
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=username=app \
  --from-literal=password='S3cr3t!'
kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=bot --docker-password=TOKEN

# base64 is NOT encryption:
kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
sections.title: Creating and consuming
sections.output:
secret/db-creds created
secret/web-tls created
secret/regcred created
S3cr3t!
sections.note: The last command prints the plaintext password for anyone with `get` on Secrets.

sections.title: A Pod that mounts a Secret
sections.body: This is a Pod manifest, `secret-demo`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, that uses the `db-creds` Secret in two ways. `secretKeyRef` injects the password as the `DB_PASSWORD` variable, and the `secret` volume mounts each key as a file under `/etc/creds` with mode `0400` (owner read-only). The output shows the files, the variable, and that the mount is a `tmpfs` held in memory.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    env:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-creds
          key: password
    volumeMounts:
    - name: creds
      mountPath: /etc/creds
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: creds
    secret:
      secretName: db-creds
      defaultMode: 0400
sections.title: Pod using a Secret
sections.output:
$ kubectl exec secret-demo -- ls -l /etc/creds
total 0
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            15 Mar 10 09:41 password -> ..data/password
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            15 Mar 10 09:41 username -> ..data/username
$ kubectl exec secret-demo -- cat /etc/creds/password
S3cr3t!
$ kubectl exec secret-demo -- printenv DB_PASSWORD
S3cr3t!
$ kubectl exec secret-demo -- df /etc/creds
Filesystem           1K-blocks      Used Available Use% Mounted on
tmpfs                  3951012         8   3951004   0% /etc/creds
sections.note: Mounted Secrets live in a tmpfs (memory), never written to node disk. Files update eventually; env vars do not.

sections.title: The decoded result in the container
sections.body: This is not a file you apply. It shows what the `secret-demo` Pod sees: the two files under `/etc/creds` and the `DB_PASSWORD` variable. Notice that the values are already decoded, so the application never handles base64 itself.

sections.code:
# /etc/creds/username  (mode 0400, no trailing newline)
app

# /etc/creds/password
S3cr3t!

# environment
DB_PASSWORD=S3cr3t!
sections.title: What the container sees
sections.note: Files hold the decoded value; Kubernetes decodes base64 for you in both env vars and volumes.

sections.title: Secrets in a Deployment
sections.body: This is a Deployment manifest, `api`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, that combines three Secrets. `imagePullSecrets` uses `regcred` to pull the private image, `envFrom` with `secretRef` turns every key of `db-creds` into an environment variable, and the `web-tls` volume mounts the certificate files at `/etc/tls`. It shows how Secrets are used in a realistic workload.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.2
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: db-creds
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /etc/tls
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: web-tls
sections.title: Deployment using a Secret and pull secret
sections.output: deployment.apps/api created
sections.note: envFrom with secretRef creates env vars named after the keys: username and password.

sections.title: Base64 is not encryption
sections.body: By default Secrets are stored **unencrypted in etcd**. Anyone with etcd access, backup access, or RBAC `get`/`list` on Secrets (or permission to create a Pod in the namespace and mount it) can read them. Never commit Secret manifests to Git in plain form.

items.title: Limit access with RBAC
items.body: Grant `get`/`list`/`watch` on Secrets only where needed; `list` reveals every value in a namespace.

items.title: Enable encryption at rest
items.body: Configure an `EncryptionConfiguration` on the API server (ideally with a KMS provider).

items.title: Prefer volumes over env vars
items.body: Env vars leak through crash dumps, `docker inspect`-style tooling and child processes.

items.title: Keep them out of Git
items.body: Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS or an external secrets operator (Vault, cloud secret managers).

items.title: Rotate regularly
items.body: Version Secret names and roll Pods when credentials change.

questions.question: Base64 encoding of Secret values provides...
questions.explain: Base64 is trivially reversible; it exists to represent binary data in YAML/JSON.

questions.question: Which type is used for registry pull credentials?
questions.explain: dockerconfigjson Secrets are referenced from imagePullSecrets.

questions.question: How do you protect Secrets stored in etcd?
options: Enable encryption at rest on the API server
questions.explain: EncryptionConfiguration (optionally with a KMS provider) encrypts Secrets before storing them.

questions.question: Why are mounted Secret volumes preferred over env vars?
options: Env vars can leak via dumps and child processes, and volumes can update
questions.explain: Volumes avoid process-environment leakage and receive updates.

lessons.title: Persistent storage
lessons.summary: Volumes, PersistentVolumes, claims, StorageClasses, access modes, reclaim policy and dynamic provisioning.
objectives: Distinguish ephemeral volumes from persistent ones
Explain the PV, PVC and StorageClass relationship
Choose access modes and reclaim policies
Use dynamic provisioning and a PVC in a Pod

sections.title: Containers forget
sections.body:
A container's filesystem disappears when it restarts. Kubernetes **volumes** outlive containers: `emptyDir` lasts for the Pod's lifetime (scratch space, shared between containers), while **persistent** volumes outlive the Pod entirely.

Persistent storage is split in two roles. A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a piece of storage in the cluster, a cluster-scoped resource. A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a namespaced request for storage by a user. Kubernetes binds a claim to a matching PV, and Pods reference the claim, never the PV.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: StorageClass and dynamic provisioning
sections.body:
A **StorageClass** describes a kind of storage (SSD, replicated, ...) and the provisioner that creates it. When a PVC names a class, the provisioner creates a PV automatically: **dynamic provisioning**. A class marked default is used when the PVC omits `storageClassName`.

`volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until a Pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in the right zone.

sections.title: A StorageClass in YAML
sections.body: This is the manifest for a StorageClass named `fast-ssd`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. It tells Kubernetes which driver (`provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com`) and settings (`type: gp3`) to use when a claim asks for storage. Look at `reclaimPolicy`, `allowVolumeExpansion` and `volumeBindingMode`, which control what happens on deletion, resizing and timing.

sections.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "false"
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
reclaimPolicy: Delete
allowVolumeExpansion: true
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
sections.title: StorageClass manifest
sections.output: storageclass.storage.k8s.io/fast-ssd created
sections.note: The provisioner and parameters are driver specific; this sample uses the AWS EBS CSI driver.

sections.title: A manually created PersistentVolume
sections.body: This is a PersistentVolume manifest, `pv-manual-10g`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. It describes 10Gi of storage that an administrator provides by hand, here a `hostPath` folder on the node, which is only suitable for test clusters. Look at `storageClassName: manual` and `Retain`: a claim must use the same class to bind to it.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-manual-10g
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/pv-manual-10g
sections.title: PersistentVolume manifest (static)
sections.output: persistentvolume/pv-manual-10g created
sections.note: hostPath is for single-node test clusters only. A PVC with storageClassName: manual and a request up to 10Gi can bind to it.

sections.title: Claiming the volume
sections.body: This is a PersistentVolumeClaim manifest, `manual-claim`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. A claim is a request for storage: it asks for 10Gi with `ReadWriteOnce` access and class `manual`, which matches the PV we just created. Kubernetes then binds the two together.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: manual-claim
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: manual
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
sections.title: PVC that binds the static PV
sections.output: persistentvolumeclaim/manual-claim created

sections.title: Seeing classes, volumes and claims
sections.body: These commands list StorageClasses, PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims. We run them to check that the claim and volume found each other. In the output, look for `Bound` in the STATUS column and the CLAIM column of the PV, which names the claim using it.

sections.code:
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get pv
kubectl get pvc

pvc-5e1c2a7d-9b34-4f10-8d2a-6a0b7c93e1f4   5Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    default/data-pvc       standard       12m

sections.title: Dynamic storage for a database Pod
sections.body: This file holds two objects separated by `---`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. The first is a 5Gi claim `data-pvc` with no PV prepared by hand: the `standard` class creates one automatically. The second is a Pod `db` that mounts the claim at `/var/lib/postgresql/data` through `claimName`, so the database files live on durable storage.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  containers:
  - name: db
    image: postgres:16
    env:
    - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
      value: example
    - name: PGDATA
      value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: data-pvc
sections.title: PVC and a Pod that uses it
sections.output:
persistentvolumeclaim/data-pvc created
pod/db created

$ kubectl get pvc data-pvc
NAME       STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
data-pvc   Bound    pvc-5e1c2a7d-9b34-4f10-8d2a-6a0b7c93e1f4   5Gi        RWO            standard       40s
sections.note: The PVC stays `Pending` until bound. With `WaitForFirstConsumer` that is normal until the Pod is scheduled.

head: Policy
Result
Sample STATUS after PVC delete
rows: PV and the backing storage are removed (default for dynamic provisioning)

sections.title: What happens when a claim is deleted
sections.body: These commands delete the claim `manual-claim` and then check the PV it was using. We run them to see the `Retain` policy in action. In the output, the PV status changes from `Bound` to `Released` and still names the old claim, so its data is kept.

sections.code:
kubectl delete pvc manual-claim
kubectl get pv pv-manual-10g
sections.title: PV reclaim output
sections.output:
persistentvolumeclaim "manual-claim" deleted
NAME            CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS     CLAIM                  STORAGECLASS   AGE
pv-manual-10g   10Gi       RWO            Retain           Released   default/manual-claim   manual         9m
sections.note: A Released PV still references the old claim; clear spec.claimRef to make it Available again.

sections.title: Deleting a PVC can delete data
sections.body: With a `Delete` reclaim policy the underlying disk is destroyed with the claim. For important data use `Retain`: `kubectl patch pv NAME -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'`. For databases prefer a StatefulSet with `volumeClaimTemplates` so each replica gets its own PVC.

sections.title: Troubleshooting a claim
sections.body: These commands are the standard checklist for storage problems: list classes, list claims and volumes, describe the claim `data-pvc`, and read its events. Use them when a Pod is stuck waiting for a volume. In the output, check the `Status`, the bound volume name, `Used By`, and the events at the bottom for provisioning errors.

sections.code:
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get pvc,pv
kubectl describe pvc data-pvc
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=data-pvc

sections.title: Testing that data survives
sections.body: These commands write a file `marker.txt` into the database directory, delete the Pod, recreate it from `db-pod.yaml` and read the file back. This is the practical proof of why PVCs exist. If the final command prints `hello`, the data outlived the Pod.

sections.code:
kubectl exec db -- sh -c 'echo hello > /var/lib/postgresql/data/marker.txt'
kubectl delete pod db
kubectl apply -f db-pod.yaml
kubectl exec db -- cat /var/lib/postgresql/data/marker.txt
sections.title: Proving data persists
sections.output:
pod "db" deleted
pod/db created
hello
sections.note: The Pod was replaced, yet the file survived because it lives on the PVC.

options: The Pod directly by PV name
questions.explain: Pods reference claims, and the claim binds to a PV.

questions.question: What does dynamic provisioning require?
questions.explain: A PVC naming a StorageClass triggers its provisioner to create a PV.

questions.question: Which reclaim policy preserves data after the PVC is deleted?
questions.explain: Retain keeps the PV and data; the PV becomes Released and needs admin cleanup.

questions.question: ReadWriteOnce means...
questions.explain: RWO allows mounting read-write by one node; ReadWriteOncePod restricts to one Pod.

lessons.title: ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges
lessons.summary: Govern a shared cluster per namespace: cap aggregate usage with quotas and set per-container defaults with limit ranges.
objectives: Write a ResourceQuota for compute and object counts
Set default requests/limits and bounds with a LimitRange

sections.title: Two tools, two scopes
sections.body:
In a shared cluster one team can starve the others. Kubernetes governs this per namespace with two objects:

- A **ResourceQuota** caps the **aggregate** consumption of a namespace: total CPU/memory requests and limits, storage, and object counts.
- A **LimitRange** constrains **individual** objects: default requests/limits for containers that omit them, plus min and max values per container, Pod or PVC.

They work together: once a quota covers `requests.cpu` or `limits.memory`, every new Pod must specify them, and a LimitRange default supplies them automatically.

sections.title: A quota for a whole namespace
sections.body: This is a ResourceQuota manifest, `team-a-quota`, applied with `kubectl apply -f quota.yaml`. It sets a ceiling on the total resources the `team-a` namespace may use. Look under `hard`: totals for CPU and memory requests and limits, plus object counts such as `pods`, `persistentvolumeclaims` and `services.loadbalancers`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "20"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
    requests.storage: 100Gi
    services.loadbalancers: "1"
sections.title: ResourceQuota
sections.output: resourcequota/team-a-quota created
sections.note: Quota is enforced at admission time. Existing Pods are never evicted when a quota is lowered.

sections.title: Common ResourceQuota fields
head: Field
Example
Constrains
rows: Sum of CPU requests of all Pods
Sum of memory limits of all Pods

sections.title: Defaults and bounds per container
sections.body: This is a LimitRange manifest, `container-defaults`, applied with `kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml` in the `team-a` namespace. It works per container, unlike the quota which works per namespace. `defaultRequest` and `default` fill in missing values, and `min` and `max` set the smallest and largest values allowed.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: container-defaults
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    min:
      cpu: 50m
      memory: 64Mi
    max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: 2Gi
sections.title: LimitRange
sections.output: limitrange/container-defaults created
sections.note: `defaultRequest` and `default` fill in missing requests and limits; `min`/`max` reject Pods outside the bounds.

sections.title: What a LimitRange does to a Pod
head: Pod spec as written
Result after admission
rows: request copied from the limit (cpu: 1) unless defaultRequest applies to unset fields

sections.title: A Pod that breaks the maximum
sections.body: This command tries to start a Pod `huge` in `team-a` with a CPU limit of 4, which is above the LimitRange maximum of 2. We run it to see the rule being enforced. The error message names the broken rule: `maximum cpu usage per Container is 2, but limit is 4`.

sections.code: kubectl run huge -n team-a --image=nginx:alpine --limits=cpu=4
sections.title: Pod rejected by LimitRange
sections.output: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "huge" is forbidden: maximum cpu usage per Container is 2, but limit is 4
sections.note: Note: on newer kubectl, `--limits` is removed; use a manifest with resources.limits.cpu: "4" for the same result.

sections.title: A Pod that exceeds the quota
sections.body: This command creates a Pod `big` that requests 3 CPUs, using `--overrides` to set resources inline. The namespace already uses 3500m of its 4 CPU request quota, so it does not fit. The error lists what was requested, what is used and what the limit is.

sections.code: kubectl run big -n team-a --image=nginx:alpine --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"big","image":"nginx:alpine","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"3"},"limits":{"cpu":"3"}}}]}}'
sections.title: Pod rejected by ResourceQuota
sections.output: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "big" is forbidden: exceeded quota: team-a-quota, requested: requests.cpu=3, used: requests.cpu=3500m, limited: requests.cpu=4

sections.title: A Pod with no resources set
sections.body: This command starts a plain nginx Pod with no CPU or memory values. Because the quota covers requests and limits, every Pod must declare them. The error lists the missing fields; a LimitRange with defaults avoids this.

sections.code: kubectl run plain -n team-a --image=nginx:alpine
sections.title: Quota without a LimitRange
sections.output: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "plain" is forbidden: failed quota: team-a-quota: must specify limits.cpu for: plain; limits.memory for: plain; requests.cpu for: plain; requests.memory for: plain
sections.note: This is what happens when no LimitRange supplies defaults.

sections.title: Checking the injected defaults
sections.body: This command prints the `resources` section of a Pod named `probe` that was created without any resource values. We run it to see the LimitRange at work. The output shows the `requests` and `limits` that were added automatically, matching `defaultRequest` and `default`.

sections.code: kubectl get pod probe -n team-a -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
sections.title: Defaults injected into a Pod
sections.output: {"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"512Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"}}

sections.title: Setting up and monitoring the namespace
sections.body: These commands create the `team-a` namespace, apply `quota.yaml` and `limitrange.yaml`, and then inspect them. `describe resourcequota` shows Used versus Hard for each resource, and `describe limitrange` shows the defaults and bounds. The last command lists events with reason `FailedCreate`, where rejections from the quota appear.

sections.code:
kubectl create namespace team-a
kubectl apply -f quota.yaml -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl describe resourcequota team-a-quota -n team-a
kubectl describe limitrange container-defaults -n team-a
kubectl get events -n team-a --field-selector reason=FailedCreate
sections.title: Checking usage
sections.output:

sections.title: Rejected Pods look like missing Pods
sections.body: When a quota is exceeded, the API rejects the Pod (a bare Pod errors on create). With a Deployment the Pod is never created and the ReplicaSet records a `FailedCreate` event such as `exceeded quota`. Check `kubectl describe rs` and the namespace events.

sections.title: Always pair them
sections.body: Apply a LimitRange alongside every compute quota. Without defaults, Pods that omit requests/limits are refused with `must specify limits.cpu`.

questions.question: Which object sets default container limits?
questions.explain: LimitRange supplies defaults and min/max per object.

questions.question: A ResourceQuota constrains...
options: The aggregate usage of a namespace
questions.explain: Quotas cap total consumption and object counts in a namespace.

questions.question: A quota on limits.memory exists and a Pod omits memory limits with no LimitRange. What happens?
questions.explain: Pods must specify the quota-tracked resources, or a LimitRange must default them.

questions.question: You lower a quota below current usage. What happens to running Pods?
options: They keep running; new ones are rejected
questions.explain: Quota is enforced only at admission; existing objects are untouched.
